 MC EXCLUSIVE Next two years will be about survival, not winning for crypto exchanges: Ethereum co-founder Vitalik Buterin warns amid rising hacks
 If hacking remains a problem, then regulators will step in and start putting responsibility on companies to be more conservative, Buterin told Moneycontrol in an exclusive interview 
 Debangana Ghosh 
 November 04, 2026 / 16:52 IST Share --> 
 --> 
 --> 
 --> 
 Vitalik Buterin, co-founder, Ethereum Foundation Vitalik Buterin praised India's growing developer ecosystem.
 Lean Ethereum uses ZK and AI to boost security and speed.
 Exchanges must adopt bunker mode to prevent cyberattacks.

 It has been a few days since Vitalik Buterin, Ethereum co-founder and one of the most influential voices in the global crypto industry, arrived in India. Much of his time here was spent fasting, almost 76 hours, he says, an annual ritual observed during every Devcon 8, Ethereum’s flagship annual conference.
 As he sat down for a conversation with Moneycontrol in Mumbai, Buterin said he was happy to see Ethereum developers here going beyond just tech privacy use cases and building for larger social good, exploring non-technical privacy, human rights and diversity.
 In a candid interview, he weighed in on the ongoing cyberattacks faced by crypto exchanges, the future of Ethereum, India's growing developer ecosystem, AI's role in blockchain innovation and why security failures could invite tighter regulation.
 Edited excerpts: Ethereum Network completed a decade last year. What’s the next 10 years going to look like for you and the blockchain platform? You have already started working towards ‘Lean Ethereum’. Tell us more about that. 
 Lean Ethereum is a set of upgrades that are happening to Ethereum over the next few years. The goal is to really properly use the latest technologies, the latest methodologies, especially including ZK (zero knowledge proofs) and then using AI and formal verification for everything. To properly push Ethereum to a place where it’s both very performant and very capable of doing the things that people want to do on top of it. But at the same time, very decentralized and very secure. Philosophically, it’s been a big shift from how Ethereum has worked before.

 AI and formal verification are really huge. The amount of work that is in the rest of this roadmap, by the standards of five years ago, would have taken us 20 years to finish. Thanks to AI, we’re able to do it so much faster and ensure that all of this code that’s being written, all of these algorithms being developed are actually safe.
 How do you envision the next generation of L1 and L2 blockchain, as your researcher Justin Drake mentioned yesterday that AI can now break cryptography without needing quantum computing? 
 Ethereum is taking a very conservative approach to this. We’re basically saying the blockchain itself is only using very conservative hash-based cryptography. Our philosophy towards L2 (layer 2), starting from this year is, that if you’re just copying Ethereum and scaling, then that’s boring and not interesting. As an L2, you should be innovating and doing something different that Ethereum by itself does not do. There are a lot of projects that do, like Lighter, which is a very high-performance DeFi protocol and various privacy protocols, like Aztec and INVAX.
 There are more examples in both of those categories, but I think high-performance DeFi and privacy are the big ones so far. Maybe the third one, if there is one, is enterprise. Enterprises can just take existing logic that’s inside their existing servers to manage supply chain records, health records, manufacturing records on chain. You basically just stick onto the chain, a hash of the data and a proof that all of the data was updated following the rules. It doesn’t decrease your privacy and improves efficiency.
 Also read:  AI is super important but don’t trust powerful corporations with your data: Ethereum co-founder Buterin 
 You had last visited India in 2023. How has the developer ecosystem evolved since then? How big is the Ethereum community in India? 
 It’s definitely continuing to grow. I see more and more people participating at every level. Even in 2023, I remember being impressed by how much progress there had been over COVID. Before COVID, I remember seeing at the very first time, there were Initial Coin Offering (ICO) tokens and they had some economic model that I did not really agree with.
 But then in 2023, I was just asked very deep questions about zero knowledge proofs and quadratic voting and proofs of personhood. From what I’ve seen so far, that trend is just continuing.
 One of the things that’s different about India is also just there’s a huge number of young people. The median age here is quite a bit under me at this point, which is the opposite of what Europe and North America and East Asia are.
 There are a lot of very curious people that are building and interested in seeing what is something meaningful that they can build right now. More emphasis on prediction markets, I’ve heard that recently, which to me makes sense. In certain sense, most of DeFi is some kind of specialized prediction market. You are either betting on the price of a dollar or you’re betting on the weather.
 Also, areas like proof of personhood protocols, trying to figure out how to interact with India’s DPI (digital public infrastructure) is continuing.
 How big is the India opportunity going to be for Ethereum? What’s your growth roadmap in the country? 
 The Ethereum Foundation’s approach is that we do what we’re good at doing, and we try to leave the things that are further from our expertise and closer to users upto the community. If we can support people and help improve security, improve privacy, improve openness, then we help technically. But otherwise, we don’t try to be masters of the whole ecosystem. So, I think ultimately, Ethereum’s Indian adoption roadmap is up to Indians.
 The Binance hack was a reminder that even the most sophisticated exchanges are vulnerable to cyberattacks and thefts, even more so in the AI era. What’s your advise to the industry on that? 
 The good news is that smart contract hacks have gone down a huge amount. All of the big hacks that we’ve seen over the last one and a half years, they’re much more concentrated in the user interface layer and in centralized components.
 On the one hand, hacks are continuing, but on the other hand, the secure core, the set of things that you can do very securely, does keep actually increasing.
 What we’ve been seeing is more and more people are realizing that their main responsibility for the next two years is not to win but to survive. Everyone is kind of figuring out what the concept of bunker mode means for them. I expect Binance will do that. I expect all of the major exchanges and custodians and institutions are also doing that.
 One good decision that Binance made is they also launched Binance Smart Chain. They also get benefit from the fact that if you do things with contracts on-chain, then you can have all these very high levels of security. I am expecting we’re going to see more moves in that direction.
 Most of these attacks both in the Bybit and Binance hacks happened remotely and done by North Korean hackers. Is there a way to control that? 
 In the long term, the only solution is that we do have to make things actually secure. The challenge is the set of things that you can do securely keeps going up and up.
 I do expect at some point if this (hacking) becomes more of a problem, then regulators will start putting responsibility on companies to be more conservative. If you get hacked and it goes to North Korea, if you go all the way to the extreme, they should treat that as donating to North Korea. Things are going to move in that direction in terms of pushing people to take things more seriously. Everyone is adapting now.
 The last step is people do have to consciously choose to do that. All of your money should be in multi-sigs. Ask security questions, we’re going to see more and more awareness on this.
 The biggest theme emerging this year in crypto is how TradFi and DeFi is converging further. Ethereum being the leader in DeFi use cases, how do you see the crypto industry shift in the next 2-3 years? Can it truly remain decentralised? 
 Ethereum is strongly leading specifically on DeFi that focuses on being high value, safe, and conservative. It’s not about the difference between 4 percent and 5 percent APY (annual percentage yield), it’s about minimizing the chance you have minus 100 percent APY.
 We’ve been seeing a lot of new things. There’s been a big growth over the last 18 months of real-world assets that are being put on Ethereum, and specifically real-world assets that in some sense have better properties in terms of security, permissionlessness, openness.
 Of course, especially with anything touching real-world assets and traditional finance from a crypto perspective, it won’t be perfect. You will still have whitelists and KYC on a lot of things, but it’s still a significant step improvement over what came before. The number of parties that are in a position to screw you over, whether in some sense of freezing access to your money or in terms of privacy, has decreased quite a bit.
 The big institutional players such as BlackRock, JP Morgan entering the crypto market also means we will see faster movements towards regulations in the US and other geographies. What’s your take on regulating crypto? Is having a common global framework a better approach? 
 That’s a tricky question. The challenge with any kind of common global regulation is that the other side of the coin will be some kind of small group of people that’s imposing their views and values on the whole world. You lose diversity, you lose the ability to see what actually happens if things are done differently. You lose choice.
 Regulations should annoy you more if you’re doing things that actually impose risk on people, and it should annoy you less or not at all if you’re doing things that impose less risk on other people. This sounds obvious, but historically there have been cases of regulation not doing even that.
